ai.literal: Hostility, they say, is to all living beings the disease that brings about the lack of good character called division.
ai.translation: Hostility, they say, is a disease for all living beings that breeds the ill disposition of division.
ai.modern: இகல் என்று சொல்லப்படுவது, எல்லா உயிர்களுக்கும் பிரிவினை என்னும் தீய குணத்தை உண்டாக்குகின்ற ஒரு நோயாகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet defines hostility (ikal) as a harmful disease (noy) that affects all living beings. It explains that hostility is the root cause of 'division' (pakal), which is described here as a complete lack of good character (panpinmai). Instead of bringing people together, hostility infects minds and creates separation, destroying the natural harmony of relationships. By comparing hostility to a disease, the poet emphasizes its destructive and infectious nature.

ai.literal: Even if they do unfriendly things intending division, not doing harmful things intending hostility is the best.
ai.translation: Even if others perform disagreeable acts to cause division, it is best to refrain from doing harmful deeds out of hostility.
ai.modern: பிரிவை விரும்பிப் பிறர் நமக்கு வெறுக்கத்தக்கவற்றைச் செய்தாலும், நாம் மாறுபாட்டைக் கருதி அவர்களுக்குத் துன்பம் செய்யாமல் இருப்பதே மிகச் சிறந்தது.
ai.explanation: This couplet advises on how to respond to provocation and attempts at division. Even when others commit unfriendly acts with the explicit intention of causing a split or discord, one must not retaliate. Refraining from doing harmful deeds out of a spirit of hostility is described as the foremost or best path. By choosing not to return harm for harm, one rises above enmity and prevents further conflict.

ai.literal: If one removes the painful disease called hostility, it will give a glory without decrease and without decay.
ai.translation: If a person rids themselves of the painful disease called hostility, it will bring them an endless and undecaying glory.
ai.modern: பகைமை என்று சொல்லப்படும் துன்பம் தரும் நோயை ஒருவன் நீக்கினால், அது அவனுக்குக் குறைவில்லாத, அழிவில்லாத புகழைக் கொடுக்கும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the immense benefit of overcoming hostility. The poet metaphorically describes hostility as a painful disease ('எவ்வநோய்') because of the constant mental and social suffering it inflicts. If one manages to cure or remove this disease, it yields a life of great glory ('விளக்கம்'). This resulting glory is described as endless ('தவலில்லா') and free from any decay or blemish ('தாவில்').

ai.literal: Within pleasure, pleasure [it] will yield, hostility called within pain pain if perishes.
ai.translation: If hostility, which is the greatest of all painful afflictions, is destroyed, it will yield the greatest of all joyful pleasures.
ai.modern: துன்பங்களுக்குள் துன்பம் என்று சொல்லப்படும் பகைமை அழிந்தால், அது இன்பங்களுக்குள் சிறந்த இன்பத்தைத் தரும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the profound impact of overcoming hostility (இகல்). The author describes hostility as the ultimate pain among all pains ('துன்பத்துள் துன்பம்'). If this supreme source of misery is completely eliminated, it naturally gives rise to the ultimate joy among all joys ('இன்பத்துள் இன்பம்'). The contrast between the greatest pain and the greatest pleasure emphasizes that peace and harmony are the true sources of human happiness.

ai.literal: Hostility against, having yielded to conduct themselves those who are capable, who indeed, to conquer desiring nature they?
ai.translation: Who indeed possesses the power to conquer those who are capable of yielding and conducting themselves peacefully when confronted with hostility?
ai.modern: பகைமைக்கு எதிராகப் பணிந்து நடக்க வல்லவர்களை வெல்ல நினைக்கும் தன்மையுடையவர் யார் இருக்கிறார்கள்? (யாரும் இல்லை).
ai.explanation: The couplet highlights the power of humility and adaptability in the face of enmity. When confronted with hostility, those who have the wisdom and strength to yield or bend rather than react with anger become invincible. The author rhetorically asks who could possibly have the capacity or nature to conquer such people. By refusing to engage in conflict and instead choosing a path of peaceful accommodation, they disarm their opponents completely, making themselves unconquerable.

ai.literal: In hostility, triumphing is sweet, he who says, his life, failing and ruining, is near.
ai.translation: The downfall and utter ruin of the life of one who thinks it is sweet to triumph in hostility are very near.
ai.modern: மாறுபாட்டில் வெல்வது இனிமையானது என்று நினைப்பவனுடைய வாழ்க்கை, தவறிப் போவதும் அழிந்து போவதும் மிக அருகில் உள்ளன.
ai.explanation: This couplet warns against the desire to dominate or triumph in a state of hostility. If a person believes that winning or asserting superiority in an ongoing feud is a sweet and desirable thing, their downfall is imminent. The poet uses two distinct terms, 'taval' (slipping or failing) and 'keṭal' (complete ruin), to show the stages of decline. The word 'naṇittu' emphasizes that this double disaster of slipping from one's position and being destroyed is not far off, but extremely close at hand.

ai.literal: Triumph attaining true reality they do not see, hostility pursuing harmful intellect they who have.
ai.translation: Those of harmful intellect who cherish hostility cannot perceive the true reality that leads to triumph.
ai.modern: பகைமையை விரும்புகின்ற தீய அறிவுடையவர்கள், தமக்கு வெற்றியைத் தரும் மெய்யான பொருளை அறிய மாட்டார்கள்.
ai.explanation: This couplet explains how hostility blinds a person's intellect. Those who harbor a harmful mind and actively pursue discord (இகல்) are unable to see the true reality (மெய்ப்பொருள்) that actually leads to lasting success or triumph (மிகல்). Their obsession with conflict prevents them from understanding what is truly beneficial, leading to their own downfall.

ai.literal: To hostility yielding is prosperity; that to increase if one desires, will hasten indeed ruin.
ai.translation: Yielding before hostility brings prosperity; but if one strives to triumph in it, ruin will surely hasten upon them.
ai.modern: பகைமைக்கு பணிந்து போவது ஒருவருக்கு ஆக்கத்தைத் தரும்; அதனை வளர்க்க விரும்பினால், அது அவருக்கு அழிவை விரைந்து கொண்டுவரும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet contrasts the outcomes of two different responses to hostility (இகல்). Yielding or bending (எதிர்சாய்தல்) when faced with enmity is presented as a wise path that leads to prosperity (ஆக்கம்), much like a reed that survives a storm by bending. On the other hand, if a person actively desires to escalate or triumph (மிகல்) in that hostility, it will surely hasten (ஊக்கும்) their own ruin (கேடு). The poet emphasizes that avoiding conflict is a source of strength, while pursuing it guarantees destruction.

ai.literal: Hostility he does not see, prosperity when coming; that, magnifying he will see, ruin to bring.
ai.translation: When prosperity is on its way, a person does not look for hostility; but when ruin is about to be brought upon him, he will seek to magnify that very hostility.
ai.modern: செல்வம் வரும்போது ஒருவன் பகைமையை நாடமாட்டான்; ஆனால் அவனுக்குக் கேடு வரும்போது, அவன் அந்தப் பகைமையை வளர்க்கவே விரும்புவான்.
ai.explanation: This couplet explains how a person's attitude toward hostility (ikal) indicates their impending fortune or ruin. When prosperity (akkam) is about to arrive, a person naturally avoids or ignores discord. Conversely, when ruin (ketu) is destined to come, the person actively seeks out and magnifies (mikal) that hostility. Thus, one's inclination to foster or avoid conflict serves as a clear sign of their future state.

ai.literal: By hostility will arise unpleasant things all; by friendliness will arise great goodness which is called abundance.
ai.translation: All painful things arise from hostility; from friendliness arises the great wealth called goodness.
ai.modern: பகையினால் துன்பங்கள் எல்லாம் உண்டாகும்; நட்பினால் நன்னயம் என்று சொல்லப்படும் பெருஞ்செல்வம் உண்டாகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet contrasts the consequences of hostility (ikal) and friendliness (nakal). The author explains that all painful and unpleasant experiences (iṉṉāta ellām) in life are born out of harboring hostility. Conversely, cultivating friendliness and joy with others yields the ultimate abundance (cerukku) which is supreme goodness (naṉṉayam). Here, 'nakal' refers to a cheerful, friendly disposition, and 'cerukku' is used in the sense of a rich abundance of virtue.
